question: Tell me about a time you used data, metrics, or analysis to drive a decision or solve a business problem.

raiseTranscript.text: I noticed our ticket resolution times were creeping up. I pulled the last 90 days of Zendesk data, grouped by category, and saw that 40% of delays came from one missing field in the intake form. I proposed a simple change, ran a two-week A/B test, and resolution time dropped 18% for those tickets.
My manager asked me to write it up for the team wiki. We rolled it out and I tracked the metric for another month to confirm it held.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you used data, metrics, or analysis to drive a decision or solve a business problem.
Situation: Zendesk ticket delays, pulled 90-day data
Action: Grouped by category, identified missing field, ran A/B test
Outcome: 18% drop in resolution time for affected tickets
Quote: "I tracked the metric for another month to confirm it held"
Follow-up: Manager asked to document; candidate wrote wiki entry and continued monitoring
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. The candidate owned a narrow but measurable slice of the support workflow and used data to isolate a root cause without overclaiming scope. The A/B test and follow-up tracking show basic analytical discipline and willingness to verify results. The story stays local to their tickets yet demonstrates coachability when the manager requested documentation. Biggest strength is the clear before/after metric tied to a simple change they proposed.

lowerTranscript.text: We had slow tickets so I looked at the numbers and suggested we fix the form. It seemed to help after we changed it.
What numbers did you look at and how did you measure the impact?
I just checked a few reports and it felt better. My manager liked the idea so we did it.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you used data, metrics, or analysis to drive a decision or solve a business problem.
Situation: Vague ticket delays
Action: "Looked at the numbers" and suggested form fix
Outcome: "Felt better," no numbers given
Quote: "I just checked a few reports and it felt better"
Follow-up: Candidate could not name specific metrics or measurement method
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. The answer never surfaces concrete data or a before/after comparison, only a feeling that the change helped. Follow-up reveals the candidate did not track or verify impact, which undercuts analytical thinking. The story lacks ownership of any specific analysis step. Primary gap is absence of measurable evidence linking data to the decision.

raiseTranscript.text: Two teams were arguing over which onboarding flow to keep. I combined signup, activation, and 30-day retention data across both flows, built a simple funnel comparison, and showed the newer flow had 12% higher activation but 9% lower retention. We ran a targeted experiment on the drop-off step and settled on a hybrid that improved retention 7 points without hurting activation.
How did you get the other team to align?
I shared the raw query and dashboard so they could rerun it. Two engineers from the other team validated the cohort logic before we decided.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you used data, metrics, or analysis to drive a decision or solve a business problem.
Situation: Cross-team disagreement on onboarding flows
Action: Combined multi-team data, built funnel, ran targeted experiment
Outcome: Hybrid flow improved retention 7 points
Quote: "I shared the raw query and dashboard so they could rerun it"
Follow-up: Candidate enabled other team to validate data before decision
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. The candidate used cross-team data to surface a trade-off, then drove an experiment that produced a measurable compromise both sides accepted. Influence came through transparent analysis rather than authority. The 7-point retention lift is credible because the candidate describes the cohort logic and validation step. Biggest strength is turning conflicting priorities into a data-backed synthesis that improved the outcome.

lowerTranscript.text: Marketing and product disagreed on the signup page. I pulled some numbers, showed a slide, and we picked one version. It performed okay.
What was the analysis and how did it change the decision?
I showed conversion rates for the two pages. Marketing agreed after seeing the slide.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you used data, metrics, or analysis to drive a decision or solve a business problem.
Situation: Marketing vs product disagreement
Action: Pulled numbers and showed a slide
Outcome: "Performed okay," no specific lift or trade-off shown
Quote: "Marketing agreed after seeing the slide"
Follow-up: Candidate could not describe how the data altered the original positions or what metric improved
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. The candidate describes presenting numbers but never explains how the analysis reconciled the two teams' positions or what concrete metric moved. No evidence of cross-team influence or experiment design. The outcome remains vague. Primary gap is lack of demonstrated analytical rigor or lasting impact beyond one slide.

raiseTranscript.text: Our support team was missing SLA targets. I had the team pull weekly cohort data on ticket volume, staffing, and resolution time. We discovered the 2-4pm window consistently understaffed. I worked with the scheduler to shift two shifts and set up a simple dashboard the leads owned. SLA attainment rose from 78% to 94% over six weeks and the team reduced escalations by 30%.
How did you handle pushback on the shift changes?
I had the leads present the data in the team meeting. Once they saw the 2-4pm gap themselves, the change felt fair and they helped communicate it.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you used data, metrics, or analysis to drive a decision or solve a business problem.
Situation: Support team missing SLAs
Action: Team pulled cohort data, identified understaffed window, shifted shifts, built dashboard
Outcome: SLA from 78% to 94%, escalations down 30%
Quote: "I had the leads present the data in the team meeting"
Follow-up: Manager enabled team to own the data and messaging
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. The candidate used data to diagnose a staffing pattern, then built a repeatable dashboard so the team could own the metric going forward. Leverage came from shifting decision-making to the leads rather than dictating changes. The 16-point SLA lift and 30% escalation drop are tied directly to the staffing adjustment. Biggest strength is developing the team's analytical capability instead of solving the problem solo.

lowerTranscript.text: Support was missing SLAs so I looked at the numbers, decided we needed more people on certain shifts, and told the scheduler. SLAs got better after that.
How did the team use the data after you made the change?
I sent the report to the leads and moved on to the next issue.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you used data, metrics, or analysis to drive a decision or solve a business problem.
Situation: Support missing SLAs
Action: Reviewed numbers and directed scheduler
Outcome: "SLAs got better," no team ownership described
Quote: "I sent the report to the leads and moved on to the next issue"
Follow-up: Candidate did not create ongoing visibility or involve team in the analysis
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for manager. The candidate used data to make a one-time decision but left no mechanism for the team to monitor or act on the metric themselves. No evidence of developing others or creating leverage through shared analysis. Outcome is stated without specifics or sustainability. Primary gap is treating data as a personal tool rather than a team capability.

raiseTranscript.text: We were debating whether to expand into a new vertical. I had finance and product build a unit-economics model using 18 months of cohort data from our closest existing segment, factoring CAC payback, LTV variance, and support cost curves. The model showed break-even at month 14 under base assumptions but negative NPV if support costs scaled linearly. We ran a 90-day pilot with capped spend and adjusted pricing mid-pilot. The pilot validated the model and we entered the vertical with a 22% higher price point that improved margin 8 points.
What trade-offs did you surface to the board?
I showed three scenarios: full rollout, pilot only, and no entry. The board chose the pilot path because the data made the downside clear if support costs weren't contained.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you used data, metrics, or analysis to drive a decision or solve a business problem.
Situation: New vertical expansion decision
Action: Built unit-economics model across 18-month cohorts, ran capped pilot, adjusted pricing
Outcome: Entered with 22% higher price, 8-point margin improvement
Quote: "The board chose the pilot path because the data made the downside clear"
Follow-up: Candidate framed three scenarios for board with clear downside visibility
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. The candidate framed a high-ambiguity market entry using cohort economics that quantified both upside and downside, then used a controlled pilot to de-risk before scaling. Strategic judgment is visible in the decision to cap spend and change pricing mid-experiment based on early data. The 8-point margin lift resulted from analysis-driven pricing rather than volume. Biggest strength is converting uncertain strategic options into comparable scenarios the board could act on.

lowerTranscript.text: We wanted to enter a new market. I asked the team to run some projections and we decided the numbers looked good enough to go ahead. It worked out fine.
What assumptions or risks did the analysis highlight?
The projections were positive so we moved forward. We adjusted later when things came up.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you used data, metrics, or analysis to drive a decision or solve a business problem.

Outcome: "Worked out fine," adjusted later
Quote: "We adjusted later when things came up"
Follow-up: Candidate could not name specific risks or how analysis shaped the go/no-go call
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for exec. The candidate relied on high-level projections without surfacing key assumptions or downside scenarios, leading to reactive adjustments after launch. No evidence of using data to make strategic trade-offs visible to stakeholders. Outcome lacks quantified business impact. Primary gap is absence of rigorous, forward-looking analysis at the level of ambiguity expected for this scope.
